nutshell: Broadcast sports video is a uniquely hard multi-object tracking setting: frequent camera switches (zoom-ins, replays, angle changes), long re-association gaps, and appearance changes across seasons/teams/jerseys break standard trackers. The paper introduces MuPNIT, the first multi-perspective NBA tracking+ReID benchmark with persistent global player identities, and Global ID Fusion (GIF), an online tracking-with-identification framework that maintains a global ID embedding database and re-links fragmented tracklets to it in a single pass, without offline post-processing.
contributions: MuPNIT: the first large-scale multi-perspective MOT+ReID benchmark for sports (2.19M boxes, 283K frames, 78.5 min of broadcast NBA video across six seasons), explicitly capturing broadcast-style camera switches, long re-association gaps, and cross-season appearance changes (teams, jerseys, lighting) that single-camera MOT datasets like MOT17/MOT20/DanceTrack/SportsMOT do not.

MuPNIT-ReID and MuPNIT-ReID-light: companion ReID datasets (396K / 55K images, 211 identity-disjoint players) with a gallery deliberately sourced from a different domain (public team/media photos) than the in-game query tracklets, enabling zero-shot cross-domain ReID evaluation with text, uniform, and pose attributes not present in prior ReID benchmarks.

Global ID Fusion (GIF): a modular tracker + ID module + global-linking architecture that maintains one fixed embedding per identity in a global ID database and re-associates tracklets that fail motion/IoU matching via cosine similarity to that database - an online, single-pass alternative to prior offline tracklet-merging approaches (e.g., GTA).

Five new 'Global ID' metrics (FTFI, FTFIc, IDsw, MCorr, mAP) that separately quantify how fast a correct identity is established versus how stable it stays over a tracklet, surfacing a tradeoff that standard HOTA/IDF1 does not capture on its own.
deficiencies: The headline abstract claim ('+25.3% HOTA, +79.5% IDF1 over OC-SORT') comes specifically from the easier 'game context' evaluation in Table 5, where the candidate identity pool is restricted to only the players actually in that specific game (requiring a known roster in advance) - in the harder, more realistic 'global context' (all identities in the test set), the same method's gains are much smaller (+13.6% HOTA, +44.0% IDF1), and the abstract does not disclose which setting its headline numbers come from.

The paper's own Table 10 shows the existing offline method GTA clearly beats GIF on the three primary tracking-identity metrics (HOTA 48.740 vs. 41.520, AssA 30.570 vs. 22.138, IDF1 52.169 vs. 42.666), with GIF only ahead on DetA and MOTA - GIF's real advantage is being online/real-time (39.47ms vs. GTA's offline post-processing) rather than being more accurate, a distinction the abstract's 'achieves state-of-the-art' framing does not make explicit.

In the cross-sport generalization test (Table 9), adding Global Linking on SoccerNet actually decreases HOTA (-1.8%), AssA (-3.3%), and MOTA (-0.8%), with only IDF1 improving (+1.3%) - the text describes this as GL 'still yield[ing] clear gains,' which understates that half of the reported metrics got worse on this dataset, not merely showing 'limited' improvement.

The global-context evaluation drops the text-attribute signal entirely ('text is omitted in the global context since it already encodes video-specific cues'), while the easier game-context evaluation keeps it - meaning the two settings being compared throughout the paper aren't just differing in candidate-pool size, they also differ in which input modalities are available, confounding the game-vs-global comparison.

All reported tracking and ReID results are single-run figures with no variance or seed reporting, despite several generalization gains in Table 9 being under 2 points (e.g., SportsMOT basketball HOTA: 73.361 -> 73.502).
notable: Table 5's own Global ID metrics surface a genuine, underexplored tradeoff: configurations with fewer ID switches, higher MCorr, and higher mAP (i.e., more stable, more accurate identification) consistently take longer to establish the correct identity in the first place (worse FTFI/FTFIc) - useful for anyone designing similar detect-then-identify pipelines, since it means 'fast to decide' and 'stable once decided' pull in opposite directions and can't be jointly maximized by the same design choice (e.g., feature-averaging window size). Also notable: the comparison with GTA (Table 10) is handled more honestly than the abstract - it directly shows an offline competitor winning on the core metrics and frames GIF's real contribution as the online/real-time property (only 19.5% latency overhead vs. the base tracker) rather than raw accuracy.
